newsitem.title: USA: Senate votes to raise Medicare retirement age.
newsitem.headline: Senate votes to raise Medicare retirement age.

text.p: The Senate voted Tuesday to gradually increase the Medicare eligibility age to 67 from the current 65, in a signal lawmakers might take some politically tough steps to ensure the program's solvency.
The Senate backed the change by a 62-38 vote. Twelve Democrats supported the increase, five Republicans voted no.

The higher eligibility age would be phased in slowly, not fully taking effect until 2027. That means people now age 59 would not be affected. Those 36 and younger would face a full two-year delay before they could begin collecting benefits.

The strong vote showed a surprising willingness by senators to buck the powerful elderly voting bloc and address the long-term financing problems of Medicare after the politically charged 1996 campaign when Democrats attacked Republicans relentlessly on the issue.

But passage was far from assured. The White House had not signed on the proposal and there may not be as much support for raising the age limit in the House which did not include a similar provision in its version of the Medicare legislation.

Supporters argued the change would bring Medicare eligibility in line with Social Security and begin needed structural reforms to protect Medicare's long-term financial health in the next century as the baby boomers retire.
They argued delaying eligibility was fair in part because life expectancy had increased since Medicare's founding.

"This is a very, very modest approach to an extremely serious problem. What we were concerned about is the solvency of Medicare," said Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican.

Pennsylvania Republican Sen. Rick Santorum, 38, the youngest member of the Senate, said Americans needed to sacrifice to protect Medicare -- not just for current recipients but his generation as well.
"What we're talking about here is being responsible, not standing up and demagoguing to get votes back home," he said.
Senior citizens' groups opposed the move as a erosion of the government's commitment to Medicare, which provides health insurance to 38 million Americans.
"Many of the people who proposed this frankly don't care much for Medicare. That came out during the last campaign," said Illinois Democratic Sen. Richard Durbin.

The White House complained the change was not part of the original balanced budget deal worked out with Congress, expressing concern some retirees might not be able to find affordable, private insurance between the ages of 65 and 67.

"There's a difference between a senator ... and the worker that's out there on the line day after day after day," complained Iowa Democratic Sen. Tom Harkin. "(This) sticks it right in their back one more time."
The underlying Medicare legislation will keep the programme solvent for nearly a decade, but the long-term financial prognosis is questionable without major structural changes.
Earlier Tuesday, the Senate blocked a Democratic effort to delete a new $5 co-payment for Medicare home health visits.

Opponents said the charge was more than many seniors could afford. But supporters said it was needed to get a handle on escalating costs in home health care, one of the fastest growing areas in Medicare.
The Senate was also expected to debate a plan that would force better-off Medicare recipients to pay higher monthly premiums for Part B doctor's coverage.

The action came as the Senate debated massive legislation reducing Medicare spending by about $115 billion over five years and cutting the Medicaid programme for the poor, elderly and disabled by $13.6 billion.
